1 / 91
A · Gradient An edge is a peak in the derivative
1

Read the intensities along a line: 20, 20, 20, 90, 160, 160, 160.

2

Take the difference of neighbors Gx ≈ I(x+1) − I(x−1) → 0, 70, 140, 70, 0.

3

The biggest value — 140 at p3 — marks the edge.

💡

Flat run → difference ≈ 0 · a jump → a peak. Finding edges = finding that peak.

1 / 91
A · Gradient Derivative ≈ difference of neighbors → Gx & Gy
1

A pixel grid has no true derivative — approximate it: slide [−1,0,+1] across a row → horizontal change Gx.

2

Slide the same kernel down a column → vertical change Gy.

🧭

Gx large ⇒ vertical edge · Gy large ⇒ horizontal edge — the edge runs perpendicular (⟂) to the change.

🌱

Every pixel now carries (Gx, Gy) — the pair we combine next. This kernel is the seed of Sobel.

1 / 91
A · Gradient The gradient has a magnitude and a direction

|∇I| = √(Gx²+Gy²) = √(3²+4²) = 5 — the edge strength.

θ = atan2(Gy, Gx) = atan2(4,3) ≈ 53° — the edge orientation (∇I points across the edge; the edge runs perpendicular (⊥) to it).

🚀

What next: threshold |∇I| → an edge map (the widget next) · Canny thins & links them into clean contours · the direction steers non-max suppression (sub-topic C) and the feature descriptors later today.

1 / 91
A · Gradient Try it: the edge threshold

edge pixels: –

Raise T and the weak noise specks fade first; the strong square edge survives longest. Push T too high and even real edges vanish — this is why Canny uses two thresholds (hysteresis).

import cv2, numpy as np
from skimage.data import camera
from google.colab.patches import cv2_imshow
img = camera()
gx = cv2.Sobel(img, cv2.CV_64F, 1, 0)
gy = cv2.Sobel(img, cv2.CV_64F, 0, 1)
mag = np.hypot(gx, gy)
cv2_imshow((mag/mag.max()*255).astype(np.uint8))
📐

The gradient measures how fast intensity changes — big magnitude = an edge.

Canny

A multi-step pipeline for clean edges.

pipeline หาขอบหลายขั้น

Non-max suppression

/nɒn ˈmæks/

1 / 91
B · Edge Detection Sobel kernels estimate Gx and Gy

The kernel sits on the patch, each cell is multiplied by the weight beneath it, and the nine products are summed — that single number is Gx at the centre pixel.

The middle column is ×0, so only the left-vs-right contrast counts → a large |Gx| = a vertical edge. Flip it (bright-left / dark-right) and Gx = −640 — same strength, the sign just says which side is brighter. Sobel-y = Kxᵀ → horizontal edges.

1 / 91
B · Edge Detection Why the [1, 2, 1] weighting?
🔙

Recall Session 3: [1,2,1] is the Gaussian-blur weight you already used; separable = a 2-D kernel is two 1-D kernels.

Why smooth first? A row = dark 20 → bright 180. Plain [−1,0,1]: 180−20 = 160. Noise flips one pixel 180→100, so that row = 100−20 = 80 (half!).

methodclean+ noiseerror
no smooth · 1 row180−20=160100−20=80−50% ✗
Sobel [1,2,1] · 3 rows640560−12% ✓

Sobel averages 3 rows: 1·160+2·160+1·80 = 560 (clean 640) — only ~12% off. The edge survives.

1 / 91
B · Edge Detection The Canny pipeline — five steps
Sobel — one quick pass (this is Canny's step ②)

Sobel outputs the magnitude; a single threshold binarizes it — Canny uses two (hysteresis). These thresholds (and the kernel size) are hyperparameters — you tune them, they are not learned.

Canny — five steps for clean, thin edges
🧩

Canny chains techniques you already know — it smooths twice (a strong Gaussian ①, then Sobel's own [1,2,1] ②), takes the gradient, then thins & links. Each step cleans the edges further.

1 / 91
B · Edge Detection Non-max suppression & hysteresis
③ Non-max suppression
1

Look along the gradient direction at each edge pixel.

2

Compare it with its two neighbours on that line.

3

Keep it only if it is the local max, else set it to 0 → a 1-px ridge.

full step-by-step in sub-topic C (s25–27)

④ Double threshold + ⑤ hysteresis
④

Two thresholds — hyperparameters you tune (T_high=80, T_low=40) — sort pixels: strong ≥80 · weak 40–80 · drop <40.

⑤

A weak pixel survives only if a chain links it to a strong seed — e.g. 90(strong)→55→50→45 all touching → kept ✓; a lone 50 → dropped ✗.

isolated weak pixels (e.g. 50 in the grass) are dropped → clean, connected edges

1 / 91
B · Edge Detection Raw gradient → Sobel → Canny
⚖️

Same photo, three tools: each added step ([1,2,1] smoothing, then the pipeline) removes more noise. Use Sobel for a quick gradient, Canny when you need clean edges to build on.

C · Non-Max Suppression Key Terms — Non-Maximum Suppression

NMS

/nɒn ˈmæks.ɪ.məm/

Keep a pixel only if it beats its 2 adjacent neighbors → write to a new map.

เก็บถ้าชนะเพื่อนบ้านที่ติดกัน 2 ตัว → เขียนลง map ใหม่

Gradient direction

/ˈɡreɪ.di.ənt/

The axis across the edge, atan2(Gy, Gx).

ทิศตั้งฉากกับขอบ

Local maximum

/ˈloʊ.kəl/

A pixel ≥ its two adjacent (touching) neighbors along a line.

จุดที่ ≥ เพื่อนบ้าน ที่ติดกัน 2 ตัว

Ridge

/rɪdʒ/

The 1-pixel line of true edge pixels.

เส้นสันขอบหนา 1 pixel

1 / 91
C · Non-Max Suppression Keep the crest, drop the slopes

At each pixel, compare it to its 2 neighbors along the gradient. Keep it only if it is ≥ both; otherwise set it to 0.

1

p2 = 80: neighbors 30 & 60 → 80 ≥ both → keep 80.

2

p1 = 30 (80 is bigger) → 0 · p3 = 60 (80 is bigger) → 0 · ends → 0.

3

Result [0, 0, 80, 0, 0] — the fat band becomes one pixel (Canny step ③).

⚠️

Compare against the original magnitudes and write to a new array — never in place, or a just-zeroed pixel would corrupt its neighbours' comparisons.

1 / 91
C · Non-Max Suppression Round the gradient to 4 directions

The angle θ is continuous, but pixels sit on a grid — round it to 4 bins.

1

θ = atan2(Gy, Gx). Bins: 0° · 45° · 90° · 135°.

2

e.g. Gx=3, Gy=4 → θ ≈ 53° → nearest bin 45°.

3

Compare only the 2 touching neighbors on that line (not all 8 in the box): 0°→L/R · 45°→↗↙ · 90°→T/B · 135°→↖↘.

🧭

direction only picks which 2 neighbors · magnitude |∇I| is the value compared (neighbors' own directions don't matter).

1 / 91
C · Non-Max Suppression Before & after NMS
Before — magnitude (a fat ridge)

cols 1–3 all high → 3–5 px thick

After NMS (compare L/R per row)

each pixel beats its 2 L/R neighbors → 1-px crest

📍

It is not “take the max of the 5”. Every pixel is tested against its left & right neighbor only — it survives if it beats both (80/86/82 do; 52 & 55 lose to 80). Survivors are written to a new grid (right); nothing is overwritten in place, so positions stay exact.

1 / 91
C · Non-Max Suppression 🌍 NMS is everywhere
📈

The fat ridge is now one clean line ✓. The same 2-neighbor rule picks peaks in 1-D signals — a sample is kept only if it beats both neighbors (audio beats, ECG R-peaks, spectrum lines). Keep the local maximum, drop the rest.

C · Non-Max Suppression
💻 LAB — Thin Edges with Canny
①Build thick edges: |∇I| threshold
②Thin them: cv2.Canny (NMS inside)
③Compare thick vs thin side by side
lab.py
import cv2, numpy as np
from skimage.data import camera
from google.colab.patches import cv2_imshow
img = camera()
gx, gy = cv2.Sobel(img,cv2.CV_64F,1,0), cv2.Sobel(img,cv2.CV_64F,0,1)
thick = (np.hypot(gx,gy) > 80).astype('uint8') * 255   # raw magnitude
thin  = cv2.Canny(img, 100, 200)                    # NMS inside
cv2_imshow(np.hstack([thick, thin]))   # thick → thin
✏️

Left = raw gradient magnitude (thick, several px) · right = Canny, where NMS keeps only the crest → 1-pixel lines. Same edges, just thinned — that is exactly NMS's job.

D · Harris Corner Key Terms — Corners

Corner

/ˈkɔːr.nər/

A point where intensity changes in all directions.

จุดที่ความเข้มเปลี่ยนทุกทิศ

Gradient sums (A, B, C)

A=ΣGx² · B=ΣGy² · C=ΣGxGy

Three sums of the window's gradients — the only inputs Harris needs.

ผลรวม gradient 3 ก้อนใน window

Eigenvalue (λ) · optional

λ = "lambda"

Advanced name for the two window-change amounts — not needed to use Harris.

ชื่อขั้นสูง (ทางเลือก) · ไม่ต้องใช้ก็หามุมได้

Harris response (R)

/ˈhær.ɪs/ · ≫ = "much greater than"

One corner score from the three sums: R=(A·B−C²)−k(A+B)²; R ≫ 0 = corner.

คะแนนความเป็นมุม · ≫ อ่าน "มากกว่ามาก"

1 / 91
D · Harris Corner Flat, edge, corner — slide the window

Nudge the little window and measure how much the pixels change (sum of squared differences, SSD) — do it in x, then in y:

measure it with sums over the window: A = ΣGx² (left–right change) · B = ΣGy² (up–down) · C = ΣGxGy (diagonal). The next slide folds A, B, C into one corner score — no matrix, no eigenvalues.

🎯

flat → change ≈ 0 every way (can't locate) · edge → big across it but ≈ 0 along it, so you cannot tell where you slid — the aperture problem · corner → big every way, the one patch you can pin down. The next slide scores exactly that.

1 / 91
D · Harris Corner The corner score — one recipe, no matrix

From the window's Gx, Gy add up 3 sums:

A = ΣGx²  left–right change

B = ΣGy²  up–down change

C = ΣGxGy diagonal coupling

corner score

R = (A·B − C²) − k·(A + B)²

k ≈ 0.04 — a hyperparameter you set (0.04–0.06)

k smaller → milder penalty → catches more corners (even blunt ones)
k larger → harsher penalty → only sharp corners survive

Three sums from the gradients you already have (Sobel) → one number R. No eigenvalues, no matrix to decompose.

1

A·B − C² is big only when both directions have gradient — a corner. For an edge one sum ≈ 0, so this term ≈ 0.

2

− k·(A + B)² pushes a strong edge below zero. Without it an edge scores 0 — same as flat — and you could not tell the two apart.

🎯

R ≫ 0 (much greater than 0, not just above it) = corner · R < 0 = edge · |R| small = flat. That is the whole detector.

1 / 91
D · Harris Corner Worked example — score one corner

Step 1 — add each pixel's gradients over the window:

pixelsGxGyGx²Gy²GxGy
1 on ┃20400
1 on ━02040
Σ440

→ A = 4 · B = 4 · C = 0

Step 2 — plug into the recipe:

R = (A·B − C²) − k·(A + B)²
  = (4·4 − 0) − 0.04·(4 + 4)²
  = 16 − 0.04·64 = 16 − 2.56 = 13.4

R = 13.4 ≫ 0 → corner ✓

1 / 91
D · Harris Corner Corner, edge, flat — one score tells them apart

R = (A·B − C²) − k·(A + B)²

caseA=ΣGx²B=ΣGy²CR
corner440+13.4
edge400−0.6
flat110+0.8

corner: (4·4−0)−0.04·8² = 16−2.56 = 13.4 · edge: 0 − 0.04·4² = −0.6 · flat: 1 − 0.04·2² = 0.8

🎯

R ≫ 0 = corner · R < 0 = edge · |R| small = flat. One number, computed from three sums — that is Harris.

1 / 91
D · Harris Corner · 🔬 optional Under the hood — the names behind the recipe

the 3 sums are a 2×2 matrix — the structure matrix M:

M = [[A, C],[C, B]] = Σ[[Gx², GxGy],[GxGy, Gy²]]

A·B − C²  =  det(M)

A + B     =  trace(M)

→ R = det − k·trace² (textbook form)

λ₁, λ₂ (eigenvalues) = the biggest and smallest amount the window changes — you never solve for them; det and trace already carry them.

termequalswhat it is for
detλ₁·λ₂big only if both directions change → the evidence for a corner
traceλ₁+λ₂total strength → the penalty that stops a strong edge faking one
same corner as slide 36, in this language:
A=4, B=4, C=0 → M = [[4,0],[0,4]]
det = 4·4 − 0² = 16  ·  trace = 4+4 = 8
R = 16 − 0.04·8² = 13.4 — the very same answer

You never need this to use Harris — the recipe already gives R. These are just the standard names you meet in papers and on the exam.

🔗

"both eigenvalues large" and "R ≫ 0" say the same thing — the recipe simply skips solving for λ.

🎯

exam: given M, take det = A·B − C², trace = A + B, then R = det − k·trace².

1 / 91
D · Harris Corner Same object, different size — can we still find it?
🔍

Harris uses a fixed window: it fits a corner on a large object, but a shrunken object fills the whole window and the corner is lost. We need detectors that work at any scale → Sub-topic E/F.

1 / 91
D · Harris Corner 🌍 Harris corners anchor panoramas
🖼️

The same corner reappears in both photos even after zoom or rotation (repeatable), so the stitcher can match it. An edge slides along itself and a flat patch looks identical everywhere — neither can be pinned down.

②Mark strong responses

lab.py
import cv2, numpy as np
from skimage.data import checkerboard
from google.colab.patches import cv2_imshow
img = (checkerboard()*255).astype(np.uint8)
R = cv2.cornerHarris(img.astype(np.float32), 2, 3, 0.04)
img2 = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_GRAY2BGR); img2[R>0.01*R.max()]=[0,0,255]
cv2_imshow(img2)
📌

Harris finds points where intensity changes in BOTH directions — corners, not just edges.

Scale-space

/skeɪl speɪs/

The image seen at multiple blur levels.

ภาพหลายระดับความเบลอ

Image pyramid

/ˈpɪr.ə.mɪd/

A stack of progressively smaller, blurrier images.

ชั้นภาพย่อ/เบลอ

Scale-invariant

/skeɪl ɪnˈveə.ri.ənt/

Detectable at any size.

ตรวจจับได้ทุกขนาด

SIFT · session 5

/sɪft/ · "Scale-Invariant Feature Transform"

The classic recipe built from this session's parts: pyramid + DoG + descriptor.

สูตรที่รวมชิ้นส่วนของคาบนี้ · ลงมือทำคาบ 5

Octave · σ

/ˈɒk.tɪv/ · σ = "sigma"

σ = how wide the blur is in pixels (not the kernel size, ≈6σ+1). One octave = σ doubling.

σ อ่าน "ซิกมา" = ความกว้างการเบลอ · octave = ช่วงที่ σ เพิ่ม 2 เท่า

1 / 91
E · Scale-Space The image pyramid — one photo at every size

We cannot resize the object — we never know its size. So resize the image, again and again, and search every level.

1

Each step: blur, then keep every 2nd pixel → side halves, pixels quarter (512²=262k → 256²=65k → …).

2

Blur first, or fine stripes collapse into fake patterns (aliasing) — the blur drops detail too small to survive the shrink.

🔺

This is what makes searching cheap. 4 sizes by growing the window: 1+4+16+64 = 85 units. On the pyramid the window never grows: 1+¼+¹⁄₁₆+¹⁄₆₄ = 1.33 — 64× less, one unchanged detector.

1 / 91
E · Scale-Space Climbing the size ladder — octaves

The pyramid alone is too coarse — it jumps ×2 a level, so an object sized between two rungs is never measured properly.

1

Climb in small steps: blur ×√2 each time; two steps and it has doubled — one octave (music: an octave doubles frequency, A 440 → 880 Hz).

2

At the top of an octave, shrink instead of blurring. Blurring to 2σ and halving the image give the same picture with ¼ the pixels — compare them on the 128 grid: corr 0.99999. Then type σ = 2 again.

3

The y-axis is size, not σ. On the half-size image one pixel is 2 old ones, so a typed σ=2 covers 4 original pixels. That is why 4 · 5.66 · 8 climbs while the typed σ resets.

E · Scale-Space 🔍 Run every level, keep the peak

The target is a round blob, the detector a fixed-size blob finder. Its size is unknown, so run the detector on every level and compare.

1

L0, L1 → 0 — the blob dwarfs the detector, which sits inside it and sees flat interior. Then 53 → 135 → 59: rise, peak, fall.

Why L3? A σ=8 detector fits radius σ√2 = 11.3. Radii per level: 80, 40, 20, 10, 5 — 10 is closest, so L3 is the characteristic scale.

🔭

Scale-space does not care what you hunt — corner, blob, template. It is only the search space; the operator that scans it is next.

explore.py
import cv2, numpy as np
img = cv2.circle(np.full((513,513), 40, np.float32),
                 (256,256), 80, 230, -1)    # one disc, r=80
s, lv = 8.0, img                  # ONE detector, never resized
for i in range(5):
    if i: lv = cv2.pyrDown(lv)   # shrink one level
    c = lv.shape[0] // 2
    g = cv2.GaussianBlur(lv, (0,0), s)
    R = -cv2.Laplacian(g, cv2.CV_32F) * s*s
    print(f"L{i} {lv.shape[0]:>3}px  resp={round(float(R[c,c])):>4d}")
▸ Output
L0 513px  resp=   0
L1 257px  resp=   0
L2 129px  resp=  53
L3  65px  resp= 135   ← peak
L4  33px  resp=  59
🔎

One detector, five image sizes — the disc only matches after shrinking 8× (L3). Try r=40 → peak moves to L2.

F · LoG / DoG A peak in the 1st derivative = a zero in the 2nd

Why bother, when the 1st derivative already shows the edge? Its peak is blunt — 80 at p4, but 40 on both sides, so you must compare neighbours and pick a threshold. A zero-crossing is a position, not a strength: no threshold to tune, and it can even fall between pixels.

1

Yes — difference the 1st derivative again. Neighbour differences 0,0,40,40,0,0 → difference those → the ∇² column:
(I₃−I₂) − (I₂−I₁) = I₁ − 2·I₂ + I₃ = [1,−2,1]
I₁, I₂, I₃ = left pixel, this pixel, right pixel — slide the window one step at a time.

atI₁ − 2·I₂ + I₃∇²I
p210 − 2·10 + 100
p310 − 2·10 + 50+40
p410 − 2·50 + 900
p550 − 2·90 + 90−40
p690 − 2·90 + 900
2

A zero alone proves nothing — p2 and p6 are 0 and flat. p4 is the edge only because +40 precedes and −40 follows: a real sign flip.

∂ is read "partial" — change along one axis, holding the other still · the ² means differentiate twice, not square.

→ no direction means no favourite direction — which is exactly what something round needs.

1

The name. ∇² is read "del squared", and the operator is called the Laplacian (after Pierre-Simon Laplace). ∇², "Laplacian" and [1,−2,1] are all the same thing in this session.

2

What it is. ∇²I = ∂²I/∂x² + ∂²I/∂y²
the curvature along x plus the curvature along y. Slide 56 did one axis; slide 59 does both.

3

What it means. It compares a pixel with the average of its neighbours: equal → 0 · brighter → negative · darker → positive. A straight ramp gives 0 too — row 2: [10,50,90] is steep, but its slope never changes, and only a change counts.

F · LoG / DoG Blur first, then Laplacian = LoG

∇² is a 2nd derivative, so it doubles down on noise — the middle panel is the proof. Smooth first, then take ∇².

1

LoG = ∇²( Gσ ∗ I )
Gσ = a Gaussian blur of width σ · I = the image · ∗ = slide it over the image.

2

Its shape is a hat — a bump in the middle, a dip all round (a sombrero). σ is how wide that hat is, and it is a hyperparameter you set.

3

Two ways to read the output: its zeros mark edges (slide 56) · its peaks, swept over σ, mark blobs and their size (slide 60). The two graphs below do both on one disc — same operator, two questions.

1 / 91
F · LoG / DoG Two axes, added — why round wins
1

∇² is the two columns added. Each is a 1st derivative differenced again — ∂²I/∂x² = ∂(Gx)/∂x — so it is Gx and Gy one step further, not Gx and Gy themselves.

2

Why a ridge loses. Along it the neighbours equal the centre → ∂²/∂y² = 0, so one axis adds nothing: −160. A blob is darker on all four sides → −320, exactly twice.

3

Sign: a bright centre gives a negative ∇², a dark one positive — polarity, not strength; code flips it so bigger = more blob-like. And a big |∇²| still only means "curved" — for round you also need the right σ (next slides).

1 / 91
F · LoG / DoG LoG fires hardest when its size matches the blob
But how do we get WHERE? The LoG is a convolution — it returns a value at every pixel, not only the one we read. Take the middle map above (σ=14.1) and read it at three places:
where you read that mapvalue
at the blob centre188← the largest in the whole image
30 px out — outside the blob (r=20)−21the dip around the hat
So WHERE = wherever the response is a local maximum — slide 70 does this over x, y and σ at once.
And a threshold is needed too: every pixel beats some neighbour, so keep a peak only if it clears a floor — the threshold=0.1 in the lab on slide 77.
Why it is written σ²·∇², not just ∇². A raw ∇² gets weaker as σ grows, so wider blobs always lose: for r = 10 / 20 / 40 the raw peaks are 5.47 / 1.38 / 0.35 — each doubling divides by 4. Multiply by σ² → 187.0 / 187.5 / 187.6: comparable at last, and the peak lands at r/√2 (7.0 · 14.2 · 28.2) instead of r/2.
You never need r. σ² uses the σ you are testing — a number you chose. r is the answer: sweep σ, take the winner, then r = σ*·√2.

A blob is a rounded patch that stands out from what surrounds it. The LoG's hat is its bump-and-dip shape — the orange circle marks how wide that hat is, and σ is the knob that sets it.

Keep the blob, sweep σ, read the response at the blob centre — * sign flipped so bigger = more blob-like; raw ∇² is negative on a bright blob (s59).

hat size σwhat it seesresponse *
4 (too small)flat interior only≈ 0
14.1 (match)the whole blob188
32 (too big)blob + background82
1

The peak sits at σ* = r/√2 → for r = 20: 20/1.414 = 14.1 ✓ exactly where the real response peaks.

🎯

So one LoG sweep gives WHERE (the centre) and HOW BIG (σ*) — that pair is a keypoint + its scale, which sub-topic G turns into something matchable.

Why 0.98 and not 1.00? Read both at the same pixels going out from the centre and divide:

px from centre051015
LoG−187−172−128−70
DoG−60.8−56.1−43.5−26.7
DoG ÷ LoG0.3240.3270.3400.381

The ratio barely moves — so the two curves are the same shape, just different heights. Theory says why: DoG ≈ (k−1) · σ² · ∇²G — ∇²G is the hat itself (the LoG) · σ² keeps different sizes comparable · (k−1) is a plain number from the ladder step (√2−1 = 0.414). A constant multiple cannot change the shape, and height never matters — we only look for extrema.

Goal: make the blob detector cheap enough to run at every scale. Same hat, no derivative — blur twice and subtract. DoG = G(σ) − G(kσ) ≈ (k−1)·LoG

1

Blurring spreads brightness outward: the peak drops, the skirt rises — so the sharper picture is taller in the middle (gap +), the blurrier taller in the skirt (gap −).

2

The hat is that gap — not the sharp picture, not the blurry one.

3

Which σ and k? Never one σ — subtract neighbouring rungs of the ladder (slide 47), so k is the ladder's step: here k = √2.

F · LoG / DoG The two pipelines side by side
🎯

Both use the pyramid — that part is shared. What differs is the next step: LoG adds a ∇² convolution to every level, DoG only subtracts neighbouring levels — and subtraction is far cheaper. Same hat either way.

1Fix the pixel, then read the DoG response there on every rung of the σ ladder.
2Compare them — slide 60's blob gave σ=4 → 0 · σ=14.1 → 188 · σ=32 → 82, so σ=14.1 wins.
3It must also beat its 8 neighbours at that rung — a maximum over (x, y, σ) together (slide 70).
4Survivors become keypoints; the circle drawn has radius σ√2 — that is the "σ that won".

F · LoG / DoG 🔍 Explore — how close is DoG, really?
explore.py
img  = cv2.imread("camera.png", 0).astype(float)
blur = lambda t: cv2.GaussianBlur(img, (0,0), t)
s    = 4.0                              # the rung we are on
log  = s**2 * cv2.Laplacian(blur(s), cv2.CV_64F)
for k in [1.10, 1.26, 2**0.5, 2.00]:   # candidate ladder steps
    dog = blur(s*k) - blur(s)      # more blurred MINUS less blurred
    c   = np.corrcoef(log.ravel(), dog.ravel())[0,1]
    print(f"{k:.2f}  {s*k:5.2f}   {c:.4f}")

1.41   5.66   0.9744   ← our ladder (s=2)
2.00   8.00   0.9040   ← rungs too far apart

Closer rungs = closer to LoG, but more levels to store and search — the whole trade-off in one column. Try it: flip to blur(s) - blur(s*k) and the correlation flips sign.

G · Blob Detection Sub-topic G in one picture
🗺️

F gave us a spot and its size. G turns it into something you can look up. The trick at every step is to remove a difference: crop by σ removes size, turning upright removes rotation, histograms of direction remove small shifts and lighting — what survives is the same 128 numbers for the same spot in any photo.

G · Blob Detection Finding blobs — one sweep, every size

Every pixel of every map is a candidate — the LoG kernel slides one pixel at a time (not in kernel-sized jumps), so every pixel already carries its own value, and the test below runs on all of them. Here is one that passes: the 3×3 patch whose centre sits on the blob centre, read at three rungs:

σ = 10 · rung below
138.0138.0138.0
138.0138.0138.0
138.0138.0138.0
9 values
σ = 14.1 · its own rung
186.6187.0186.6
187.0187.5187.0
186.6187.0186.6
the candidate + 8
σ = 20 · rung above
154.0154.3154.0
154.3154.6154.3
154.0154.3154.0
9 values

This candidate is 187.5 — best rival on its own rung 187.0 · below 138.0 · above 154.6, so it beats all 26 and survives.
One that fails: take a different pixel, 6 px off the centre — it scores 171.0 but a neighbour on its own rung has 176.0, so it is suppressed. That is why one blob leaves one keypoint, not a cluster.

“My object is not a circle.” It need not be — the detector fires wherever a small spot differs from its surroundings in every direction: corners, line ends, texture. This photo gives 2600, median size 3 px — a keypoint is never the object. The real limit is texture: a flat grey square gives 0.

Run the LoG at a ladder of σ and you get a stack of response maps — one per size. A blob is a spot that beats its surroundings in that whole stack.

1

Be a maximum in three directions: bigger than its 8 neighbours on its own rung, and than all 9 on the rung below and all 9 above — 26 in total. That is non-max suppression in (x, y, σ).

2

Every survivor is a keypoint (x, y, σ) — where it is and how big it is, from one pass.

🎯

Same operator, sizes from 2 to 12 px — nothing was tuned per star.

1 / 91
G · Blob Detection σ tells you how much to crop
Why 6σ? A Gaussian is spent by ±3σ — 99.7% of it lies inside, and out there its height is only 1.1% of the peak. So ±3σ = 6σ wide catches everything the blob touched and nothing beyond — and it runs to about 2× the blob's diameter (2σ√2 = 2.83σ): the blob plus a ring of context.
And the Gx, Gy above are not from the LoG — the LoG is a 2nd derivative with no direction (slide 57). They are computed fresh on this patch with Sobel. Two operators, two jobs: LoG → where + how big · gradient → which way up.

A keypoint is (x, y, σ) — σ says how large a piece of image belongs to it.

1

Crop about 6σ: near (σ=14) → 84 px, far (σ=7) → 42 px. Different pixels, same content.

2

Resize both to 64×64 → they line up (0.99), so any descriptor comes out the same. That is scale invariance.

3

Rotation would still ruin it — so give the patch its own "up": bin |gradient| into 8 directions, take the tallest (here 270°), then turn the patch by that angle around the keypoint so it always starts at 0°.

We cannot store raw pixels — brightness and tiny shifts would break every match. Store the pattern of gradient directions instead.

1

Cut the normalised patch into a 4×4 grid, and describe each cell by an 8-bin histogram of gradient direction.
The patch is 64×64 (slide 71), so 64 ÷ 4 = 16: every cell is 16×16 = 256 pixels. Nothing here is a free parameter except the 64 and the 4.

2

4 × 4 × 8 = 128 numbers. Finally divide by the vector's length, so turning the lights up changes nothing.

🔗

Two keypoints match when their 128-vectors are close in distance — that is the whole matching rule.

G · Blob Detection Inside one cell — how a pixel votes
Where does 16×16 come from? The normalised patch is 64×64 (slide 71) and we cut it 4×4 (slide 72) — 64 ÷ 4 = 16, so each cell is 16×16 = 256 pixels, which is why 256 votes land in the histogram.
Recap — where Gx and Gy come from (both already taught in sub-topic A): Gx, Gy = slide the Sobel kernel across a row and down a column (slide 15) · magnitude = √(Gx²+Gy²), how strong the edge is · direction = atan2(Gy, Gx), which way it points (both slide 8).

Every pixel in the cell casts one vote: its gradient direction picks the bin, its magnitude is how loudly it votes.

1

Do that for all 256 pixels and this cell leans hard on 0° and 180° — a vertical edge runs through it (gradients point across it, left and right).

🧾

These 8 numbers are the orange block from the previous slide. Sixteen cells like this, laid end to end, make the 128-number descriptor.

1 / 91
G · Blob Detection 🌍 Find this object in that photo
🔍

Nobody told the computer what a motorcycle is. It described 128 numbers per keypoint in each photo and looked for the closest vectors — that alone locates the object under a new viewpoint. Reverse image search and Google Lens are this, run over millions of photos.

1 / 91
G · Blob Detection How the search actually works

It is not template matching. Nothing slides, no pixels are compared — both photos are described independently, then the descriptions are looked up.

1

Describe both sides, then look up. Run F+G on each photo separately — query 394 keypoints, scene 2591, each already carrying its 128 numbers. Then measure one query vector against all 2591 and keep the two nearest.

⚡

Why not sliding? A template must be retried at every position, size and angle — all of which were already removed (slides 71–72). One lookup per keypoint suffices.

1 / 91
G · Blob Detection Matching — and how to reject a bad match
a candidated₁ (best)d₂ (runner-up)d₁/d₂verdict
#1423600.12✓ keep
#21203320.36✓ keep
#32542860.89✗ reject
#43393430.99✗ reject
#53483481.00✗ reject
Where do d₁ and d₂ come from? Take one query keypoint's 128-vector and measure its distance to all 2591 scene descriptors — d = √(Σ(vᵢ − wᵢ)²) over the 128 components. Sort them: d₁ = the closest, d₂ = the second closest — two different scene keypoints, the winner and the runner-up.
For candidate #1 above: closest 42, second 360, third 372, median over all 2591 546. That is what knnMatch(…, k=2) returns.

Match a keypoint by the distance between its 128-vector and each candidate's — nearest wins. But how near is near enough?

1

A fixed threshold fails — distances mean different things across a photo. Compare the best against the runner-up instead.

2

Ratio test: keep only if d₁/d₂ < 0.75. Clear: 42/360 = 0.12 ✓ · Ambiguous: 313/329 = 0.95 ✗ — the runner-up is just as good, so it is a coin flip.

🎯

That keeps 142 of 394 (36%) — the green lines on the last slide. 0.75 is a hyperparameter: lower = stricter.

gy = cv2.Sobel(patch, cv2.CV_32F, 0, 1, ksize=3)
mag = np.hypot(gx, gy)
ang = (np.degrees(np.arctan2(gy, gx)) + 360) % 360

for b in range(8):                      # 8 bins of 45°
    m = (ang >= b*45) & (ang < (b+1)*45)
    print(f"{b*45:>4}° {mag[m].sum():>9.0f}")
▸ Output
   0°  56513 · 45°  48408 ·  90°  81159 · 135°  53346
 180°  53328 · 225°  51338 · 270°  89182 ← tallest · 315°  78516
🔎

270° wins — this patch's "up". Every copy gets turned by that angle before describing. Try it: crop elsewhere and watch the winner move.

G · Blob Detection 🎯 Your Turn — Predict, Then Verify
🎯

On paper first: gradients (5, 10°) (3, 95°) (4, 20°) (2, 190°) — with 8 bins of 45°, which bin wins, and by how much?

your_turn.py
mag_ang = [(5, 10), (3, 95), (4, 20), (2, 190)]
bins = [0]*8                       # 8 bins of 45°
for m, a in mag_ang:
    bins[a // 45] += m           # which bin does the angle fall in?
print(bins, "→ winner", bins.index(max(bins))*45, "deg")
▸ Output
[9, 0, 3, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0] → winner 0 deg
✅

10° and 20° both land in bin 0 (0–45°) → 5+4 = 9, beating 95° (bin 2 → 3) and 190° (bin 4 → 2). Push further: move 20° to 50° and the winner flips to bin 1 — bin edges matter, which is why real code interpolates between them.

Summary Session Summary
Gradient
magnitude √(Gx²+Gy²) & direction atan2 — the hand-calc skill
Sobel & Canny
Sobel = fast kernel; Canny = smooth → gradient → NMS → hysteresis
NMS
thin thick ridges to a 1-pixel line along the gradient
Harris
R = (A·B − C²) − k·(A+B)² from ΣGx², ΣGy², ΣGxGy — R ≫ 0 = corner
Scale-space & LoG/DoG
zeros = edges · σ* = r/√2 = a blob's size · DoG ≈ LoG (corr 0.97) for one subtraction
Descriptors
crop by 6σ, turn upright, 4×4 cells × 8 bins = 128 numbers; keep a match only if d₁/d₂ < 0.75

✔Answer — NMS
A) [0, 0, 70, 0, 0]

p3 = 70: neighbors 40 and 40 → 70 ≥ both → keep. Every other pixel is below a neighbor → set to 0.

❌ Common mistake: comparing all 8 neighbors. NMS compares along the gradient (across the edge) — just 2 pixels.

GivenM = [5,0; 0,5], k = 0.04
det(5)(5) − (0)(0) = 25
trace²(5+5)² = 10² = 100
R25 − 0.04·100 = 25 − 4 = 21
∴ R = 21 > 0 (large) → corner

Diagonal M → eigenvalues 5, 5 (both large).

✎Checkpoint — LoG / DoG⏱ 3 min

Q1: Between which two pixels is the edge (zero-crossing)?   Q2: DoG approximates which operator?

A) p2–p3 · LoG
B) p1–p2 · Sobel
C) p3–p4 · LoG
D) p1–p4 · Harris
1 / 91
✔Answer — LoG / DoG
A) between p2 and p3 · DoG ≈ LoG

The response changes sign between p2 (+2) and p3 (−2) → the edge lies there. DoG approximates the LoG.

❌ Common mistake: picking the largest |response|. The edge is at the sign change, not the biggest value.

A) Blobs (round regions)
B) Only corners
C) Only straight lines
D) Color

Answer: A — blobs. LoG fires at the center of round regions at the matching scale. ❌ Corners are Harris's job.

🧮Worked Example — the Scale That Matches the Blob
Givena round spot of radius r = 28 px
σ*r / √2
=28 / 1.414 = 19.8
checksweep σ: 8 → 7 · 19.8 → 188 · 34 → 123
∴ σ* = 19.8 — the σ that wins is the size
1 / 91
✎Checkpoint — How Big Is the Blob?⏱ 2 min

A LoG sweep over a round spot peaks at σ = 6. What is the spot's radius?

A) 4.2 px
B) 8.5 px
C) 6.0 px
D) 12.0 px
💭

The detector reports σ; you want r. Rearrange σ* = r/√2.

1 / 91
✔Answer — How Big Is the Blob?
B) 8.5 px

σ* = r/√2  ⇒  r = σ*·√2 = 6 × 1.414 = 8.49 ≈ 8.5 px. This is how a detector reports size: it never measures the radius directly — it reports the σ that won, and you convert.

❌ Common mistake: answering 6.0 (option C) — that is σ, not r. The hat is always wider than the blob it matches, by a factor of √2.
1 / 91
✎Quick Check — Why σ²·∇² and not ∇²?⏱ 1 min

The same blob is measured at σ = 4 and at σ = 16. With a raw ∇², which is true?

A) Both give the same response
B) The larger σ answers ~16× weaker, so sizes cannot be compared
C) The larger σ answers stronger
D) σ has no effect on the response
✅

Answer: B. A raw ∇² weakens as σ², so four times the width answers 16× weaker — the sweep would always crown the smallest σ. Multiplying by σ² puts it back: measured peaks 187.0 / 187.5 / 187.6 for r = 10 / 20 / 40 (slide 60). It also moves the peak to r/√2 instead of r/2.

✎Quick Check — How Many Neighbours?⏱ 1 min

To survive as a keypoint, a spot must beat its neighbours in the response stack. How many does it compare against?

A) 8 — its own rung only
B) 10 — 8 plus the same spot above and below
C) 26 — 8 on its rung, 9 below, 9 above
D) 27 — including itself
✅

Answer: C — 26. 8 + 9 + 9: the rungs above and below are compared in full 3×3, not just at the same spot (slide 70). ❌ Comparing only within one rung would let the same spot win at every σ, so you could never pick one size.

✎Quick Check — Keep This Match?⏱ 1 min

One keypoint's two nearest descriptors in the other photo are d₁ = 281 and d₂ = 319. Keep it or throw it away?

A) Keep — 281 is the smallest distance
B) Reject — the ratio is 0.88, above 0.75
C) Keep — 0.88 is still below 1
D) Cannot tell without the 128 numbers
✅

Answer: B. 281 / 319 = 0.88 > 0.75 → the second-best is almost as good, so the "best" one means nothing. A real keeper looks like 106 / 303 = 0.35. On the rotated, shrunk cat photo only 230 of 558 pairs survive — throwing most away is the point.

1 / 91
✎Quick Check — Why Divide by the Length?⏱ 1 min

The same spot is photographed again with the lights turned up ×1.6. Before normalising, what happens to its 128-vector?

A) Nothing — gradients ignore brightness
B) It grows by about 59%, so the same spot looks like a different one
C) Only the largest entries change
D) It shrinks
✅

Answer: B. Brighter pixels mean bigger gradients, so every entry grows and the raw vector grows with them — measured, +59%. Divide each vector by its own length ‖v‖ = √(Σvᵢ²) and the two agree to corr 0.9998: the k cancels, because ‖v‖ grew by the same k. Brightness gone, pattern kept (slide 72).

Part A ✎ Hand Calculation (14 min) — Q1–Q6
Part B 💻 Code (8 min) — Q7–Q10

Topics: Gradient · Harris · NMS · LoG zero-crossing · blob scale σ* · Sobel/Canny & matching code

✎Q1 — Sobel on a Patch

Given

  • patch [10,10,10 / 10,50,10 / 10,10,10]
  • Sobel-x kernel

Find

  • Gx at the center pixel
  • the magnitude if Gy = 0
💭

Weight each column by the Sobel-x kernel, subtract left from right. Notice the symmetry.

✎Q2 — Magnitude & Direction

Given

  • Gx = 5, Gy = 12

Find

  • the gradient magnitude
  • the direction (atan2)
💭

5-12-13 is a Pythagorean triple — the magnitude comes out clean.

✎Q3 — Classify by Eigenvalues

Given

  • P1: λ₁=8, λ₂=7
  • P2: λ₁=9, λ₂=0.2
  • P3: λ₁=0.1, λ₂=0.1

Find

  • Classify each point as corner / edge / flat
💭

Both big = corner · one big = edge · both small = flat.

✎Q4 — Non-Maximum Suppression

Given

  • gradient row (direction horizontal)
  • p1..p5 = [15, 45, 90, 50, 10]

Find

  • the 5 output values after NMS
  • which pixel survives
💭

Compare each pixel with its left and right neighbors; keep only local maxima.

✎Q5 — LoG Zero-Crossing

Given

  • intensities across an edge
  • I = [20, 20, 60, 100, 100]

Find

  • apply [1, −2, 1] at p2, p3, p4
  • where is the zero-crossing (edge)?
💭

∇²I = I(left) − 2·I(center) + I(right). The edge is the sign change.

✎Q6 — Which Scale Finds This Blob?

Given

  • a round spot of radius r = 17 px
  • a σ ladder 8.0 · 11.3 · 16.0 · 22.6

Find

  • the matched scale σ*
  • which rung of the ladder is nearest
  • what the ladder's step k is
💭

σ* = r/√2 ≈ 0.707·r · each rung is the previous one times k — read 8.0 → 11.3 to get it.
